column4: Pharaoh threatens to cut and crucify the believing magicians in palm trunks, then boasts that his عَذَاب is harsher and more lasting; this is the exact human claim that the section hears 89:25-26 overturning.
Pharaoh is again called ذُو ٱلْأَوْتَادِ, the only other Quranic occurrence of his epithet “possessor of stakes,” so this directly fixes the section’s stake image to him.
فَشُدُّوا ٱلْوَثَاقَ stages the section’s وَثَاق as a firmly tightened bond; the verse’s later release or ransom also bounds this human wartime restraint against the unmatched final binding of 89:26.

ثُمَّ صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ مِنْ عَذَابِ ٱلْحَمِيمِ combines pouring, punishment, and descent from above, making literal the section’s reading of a “poured” whip as an overhead mass rather than one blow.
يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمُ ٱلْحَمِيمُ is the other exact scene of punitive liquid poured from above, matching the downward volume that the section finds in فَصَبَّ.

The liquid poured in 22:19 melts what is inside them and their skins; this verse supplies the bodily result of the preceding pour and meets the section’s account of the whip entering or mixing with the skin.
Iron maces are assigned to them immediately after the poured-liquid scene, bringing together the section’s two components: a descending mass and a striking instrument of punishment.
خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ commands that the condemned person be seized and shackled, directly staging the final binding that the section sets against Pharaoh’s power to fasten people.
The command to insert him into a chain seventy cubits long turns the section’s abstract “binding” into the immense eschatological chain it explicitly cites.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ gives failure to urge feeding the poor as a reason for the chained person’s fate, exactly joining 89:18 to the binding scene.
إِنَّ لَدَيْنَا أَنكَالًا وَجَحِيمًا locates shackles and blaze with God, directly supporting the section’s transfer of binding power from the earthly tyrant to divine judgment.
The criminals appear مُقَرَّنِينَ فِي ٱلْأَصْفَادِ, coupled together in fetters, which is the collective chain scene named in the section.
Collars around necks and chains by which the condemned are dragged concretize the section’s claim that the final وَثَاق becomes an iron chain.
Chains, iron collars, and a blaze are prepared together for the disbelievers, exactly the punitive restraint-and-fire complex invoked by the section.
Pharaoh threatens the magicians with opposite-side amputation and crucifixion, a parallel formulation of the bodily fastening power condensed in his “stakes.”
Pharaoh threatens opposite-side amputation and crucifixion and asserts that the magicians will know the result, repeating the coercive boast that 89:25-26 answers.

فَٱجْلِدُوا ... مِا۟ئَةَ جَلْدَةٍ is the Quran’s explicit scene of punishment by lashes; its word for a lash also keeps the blow at the skin, the bodily surface from which the section explains the whip’s name.
The angels are commanded to strike above the necks and every fingertip, giving a literal punitive beating to the dictionary claim that عذاب begins from striking.
Angels strike the faces and backs of the dying disbelievers while telling them to taste burning punishment, directly joining ضرب to عذاب as the section’s dictionary account does.
Angels taking the condemned while striking their faces and backs repeats the punitive beating scene and stands near 47:4’s material bond.

Every time the condemned persons’ skins are burned, they receive new skins so that they continue to taste ٱلْعَذَابَ; punishment’s repeated penetration of skin closely fits the section’s etymological image of the whip mixing into hide.
The criminal who comes to God has Hell, where he neither dies nor lives; it supplies the enduring divine outcome behind Pharaoh’s claim in 20:71 that his own عذاب is more lasting.
وَلَعَذَابُ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ أَشَدُّ وَأَبْقَىٰ gives the Quran’s direct verdict that the afterlife punishment is harsher and more lasting, answering Pharaoh’s exact comparative boast in 20:71.
God seizes Pharaoh with نَكَالَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ وَٱلْأُولَىٰ, making the tyrant who threatened punishment himself the object of exemplary divine punishment.
Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire and then ordered into أَشَدَّ ٱلْعَذَابِ, a direct Quranic answer to Pharaoh’s claim to possess the harsher punishment.
Dhu al-Qarnayn says that he will punish the wrongdoer and that God will then punish him عَذَابًا نُّكْرًا; the succession explicitly measures a ruler’s limited punishment against God’s final one.
فَيُعَذِّبُهُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْعَذَابَ ٱلْأَكْبَرَ names God as agent of “the greatest punishment,” a concise parallel to the unmatched punishment of 89:25.
Pharaoh’s people subject the Israelites to سُوءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ by slaughtering sons and sparing women, showing عذاب as a human tyrant’s inflicted violence before the divine reversal.
The same rescue memory calls Pharaoh’s slaughter and oppression سُوءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ, directly giving the “punishment” that the possessor of stakes exercised on bodies.
Moses recalls Pharaoh’s people afflicting Israel with سُوءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ through slaughter, another direct scene of the tyrant’s earthly claim to punish.
Moses and Aaron are told to demand that Pharaoh release Israel and وَلَا تُعَذِّبْهُمْ, explicitly addressing Pharaoh as the human agent of torment whom the section later sees answered.
God says He rescued the Israelites from ٱلْعَذَابِ ٱلْمُهِينِ; 44:31 identifies that degrading punishment as coming from Pharaoh, so this verse supplies the tyrant’s human عذاب.
The people of Saqar confess that they did not feed the poor, independently repeating the section’s concrete link between neglect of the needy and eschatological punishment.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ repeats 69:34’s wording almost exactly and therefore reinforces the specific offense that the section connects to the chain.
فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ makes freeing a neck the steep saving act, a precise reversal of collars, shackles, and the unbreakable punitive bond in the section.
The miserly hand is pictured as مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ, chained to the neck; this turns refusal to give into the same bodily shackle that the section associates with failure to feed the poor.
Those who hoard God’s bounty will be collared on Resurrection with what they withheld, directly joining miserliness to a neck-bound punishment as the section joins neglected feeding to chains.
A rope of twisted palm fibre around the neck supplies both an organically braided binding material and a punitive neck restraint, close to the section’s woven leather and final bond.
Those who deny resurrection are described with iron collars on their necks and as companions of the Fire, another direct eschatological binding scene.
God places collars on the necks of the disbelievers and says they are repaid only for their deeds, explicitly presenting restraint as measured recompense.
The condemned are thrown into a narrow place in Hell مُقَرَّنِينَ, bound together; confinement and binding combine into the eschatological وَثَاق image.
وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهِم مَّطَرًا makes destruction literally descend as rain, the concrete punitive downpour behind the section’s claim that “poured” enlarges a whip into a falling mass.
Stones of baked clay are rained upon Lot’s town, giving punishment the overhead weight and multiplicity that the section hears in فَصَبَّ.
The overturned town is rained upon with stones of baked clay, another direct staging of punishment as a mass descending from above.
وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهِم مَّطَرًا repeats the punitive-rain formula and then calls it an evil rain for those warned, closely matching the section’s downpour reading.
The same formula rains a destructive rain on the warned people, independently confirming the Quranic scene of punishment arriving with rain’s volume.
One compact reckoning assigns different peoples a stone storm, a blast, earth-swallowing, or drowning; it concretely matches the dictionary gloss of a “whip” mixed from multiple kinds of punishment.
وَٱلْجِبَالَ أَوْتَادًا uses the same “stakes” as stabilizing mountain-pegs; their life-sustaining firmness reverses Pharaoh’s coercive use of fastening power.
أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَاءَ صَبًّا is the Quran’s exact positive instance of water being poured, confirming the section’s lexical contrast that one pours water while a whip is ordinarily struck.
The magicians tell Pharaoh to decree whatever he can, because he can decree only this nearer life; the verse directly limits the earthly punisher whose boast appears in 20:71.
The magicians answer that God is better and more lasting, overturning Pharaoh’s immediately preceding assertion that his own punishment is harsher and more lasting.
The Messenger removes people’s burdens and the shackles that were upon them; release from binding supplies the saving opposite to the section’s final, punitive restraint.
Job is told to take a bundle in his hand and strike once without breaking his oath; a gathered striking implement used mercifully and sparingly reverses the section’s vast, poured scourge.
ٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ is the secure handhold that never breaks, using the section’s و ث ق root for a saving attachment rather than a punitive bond.
The person who submits to God is said to have grasped ٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ; this second “firmest handhold” gives divine firmness a protective direction opposite to shackling.

Crucifixion and opposite-side amputation appear here as a delimited judicial penalty for violent public crime, setting a legal boundary around the same acts Pharaoh threatens arbitrarily in 7:124 and 20:71.
وَمَاءٍ مَّسْكُوبٍ places poured water among the delights of the companions of the right; it preserves the section’s water-versus-whip distinction while reversing punitive pouring into provision.
The righteous feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite loving the food; within the same surah as the chains of 76:4, this action supplies the moral opposite of the chained man’s neglect in 69:34.
Feeding on a day of hunger continues the liberating “steep path” opened by freeing a neck in 90:13, reversing both the section’s bond and its failure to feed.
True righteousness includes giving wealth to the needy and freeing people from bondage, placing the two positive acts opposite the section’s paired neglect of the poor and punitive chaining.
This verse orders the shackled man of 69:30 into Hellfire before the chain of 69:32; its own contribution is to locate the binding inside divine punishment rather than mere custody.
The people dragged by collars and chains in 40:71 are then taken through boiling water and burned; this verse completes the cited chain’s punitive destination.

Shackles are pictured at the rejecters’ necks up to their chins, making them rigid and unable to lower their heads; although figurative in its immediate warning context, the bodily posture sharpens what binding does.

Solomon has other rebels coupled in fetters, using almost the same مُقَرَّنِينَ فِي ٱلْأَصْفَادِ as 14:49 in a temporal royal setting and thereby distinguishing delegated human restraint from final divine binding.
A stone-bearing gale is sent against Lot’s people, a non-rain formulation of the same many-projectile punishment descending with storm-like force.
The hearers are warned that God can send a stone storm upon them, turning the section’s downward punitive mass into a direct divine threat.

After boiling liquid and foul fluid in 38:57, وَءَاخَرُ مِن شَكْلِهِۦٓ أَزْوَاجٌ adds other paired kinds; its own stress on multiple varieties matches the gloss of سَوْطَ عَذَابٍ as mixed forms of punishment.
God tells believers to remember the covenant وَاثَقَكُم بِهِ, using the same و ث ق root for a binding moral commitment and thus developing the section’s secondary sense “to make firm.”
Marriage is called مِّيثَاقًا غَلِيظًا, a weighty covenant; the same root moves firmness from a physical restraint to a solemn interpersonal bond.
Those who break God’s مِيثَاق after it has been bound and cut what He ordered joined turn secure moral attachment into rupture, a meaningful abstract counterpart to material وَثَاق.
Those who fulfill God’s covenant and do not break the مِيثَاق preserve a moral bond, showing the constructive form of the firmness that becomes punitive restraint in the section.
Those who break God’s covenant after its binding and sever commanded ties repeat the concrete actions of undoing and cutting a bond in an ethical register.
Joseph foretells that one prisoner will be crucified and birds will eat from his head; it is a separate, non-Pharaonic crucifixion scene that clarifies the bodily act behind Pharaoh’s threat.
Pharaoh disobeys the messenger and God seizes him with a ruinous seizure; in the same surah as the shackles of 73:12, this makes the famous earthly captor the object of divine force.
Pharaoh’s people deny all the signs and are seized with the seizure of One mighty and fully capable, reversing the tyrant’s claim to superior coercive power without reusing the chain vocabulary.

مِن فِرْعَوْنَ identifies Pharaoh as the source of the degrading punishment named in 44:30 and characterizes him as haughty and excessive; its own role is to assign the human torment to the stake-holder.
The verse says the punishment of the afterlife is more arduous than punishment in this life and that no one shields from God, a direct scale for the section’s human-versus-divine comparison.
A nearer punishment is distinguished from the greater punishment, giving the section’s contrast between earthly blows and final punishment an explicit two-level vocabulary.
After worldly disgrace, the punishment of the afterlife is said to be greater, another explicit hierarchy that denies any earthly torment the last word.
After a storm humiliates ʿAd in worldly life, the afterlife punishment is called more humiliating, comparing a mass punishment here with the more decisive one to come.
After the garden owners’ worldly ruin, the verse states that the afterlife punishment is greater; it generalizes the section’s measure of a present affliction against final عذاب.
The person in the greatest Fire neither dies nor lives, a concise description of the endurance implicit in the claim that divine punishment outlasts Pharaoh’s.
Those who tortured believing men and women in fire face the punishment of Hell and burning; a human persecutor is thus subjected to the same kind of divine reversal the section sees for Pharaoh.
Hoarded wealth is heated and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs; this specifically joins greed to punishment impressed on the body’s surface, where the section locates the whip’s force.
A destitute person is the recipient specified after the feeding act of 90:14; this verse completes that passage’s positive reversal of failing to urge food for the miskīn.
God casts firm mountains into the earth so that it will not sway with people; this is a direct nonlexical parallel to the section’s stake as something driven into ground to hold it steady.
Firm mountains are placed in the earth specifically so that it will not shake with its inhabitants, repeating the stabilizing work expressed by the section’s stake image.
The verse again says firm mountains were cast into the earth lest it sway with people, a repeated formulation of fastening the ground through peg-like objects.
God is able to send punishment from above or from beneath people’s feet; the first alternative directly frames divine punishment as the overhead mass that the section finds in فَصَبَّ.

Fire encloses the wrongdoers, and their plea for relief brings a molten liquid that scorches faces; confinement and punitive liquid meet in one ayah as the section joins binding with poured punishment.
God takes Israel’s مِيثَاق, raises the Mount above them, and commands them to hold firmly to what they were given; covenantal binding, firmness, and an overhead mass converge in this verse.
The covenant-and-raised-Mount scene is repeated, again coupling مِيثَاق with a vast object held above the addressees and a command to take revelation firmly.
The Mount is raised above Israel because of their covenant, and the verse closes by saying God took from them a solemn covenant; it concretely joins overhead force to the و ث ق root’s moral sense.

The covenant taken from Israel explicitly includes kindness to orphans and the needy, linking the root’s moral bond to the very duty toward the poor whose neglect the section connects to punitive chains.
Expiation for a broken oath includes feeding ten needy people or freeing a person from bondage, placing feeding and release together as a precise restorative opposite to neglect followed by binding.
The criminals are seized by their forelocks and feet, a concrete bodily restraint that recalls the section’s dictionary image of a foot fixed inside a shackle.

Pharaoh’s people are cited as a people God seized for their sins, followed by the verdict that God is powerful and severe in punishment; this directly reverses Pharaoh’s boast of superior punitive force.
Immediately after Pharaoh’s crucifixion threat in 26:49, the magicians say it causes no harm because they are returning to their Lord; their stance denies the tyrant’s punishment final power.
After Pharaoh’s parallel threat in 7:124, the magicians answer that they are returning to their Lord, again setting divine destination beyond the reach of his bodily punishment.

A claim that God’s hand is fettered is answered by saying the speakers’ own hands are fettered; this rhetorical reversal specifically turns an attempted limitation of divine power back upon human beings.
Believers are commanded to hold together to God’s rope, giving a rope the saving and unifying function opposite to the punitive cords and chains developed in the section.
ʿAd mistake the approaching cloud for one that will bring rain, but it is a wind containing painful punishment; the verse makes expected rain and descending عذاب occupy the same visible mass.
Animal hides are made into light, portable dwellings, using the same hide material that the section says is braided into a whip for shelter rather than bodily punishment.
A woman who unravels her firmly spun yarn becomes the simile for undoing oaths; the verse joins braided material, achieved firmness, and the deliberate loosening of a moral bond.
Freeing a person from bondage is required before a couple resume marital contact after ẓihār; the ayah makes release from a bound neck a restorative act rather than a punishment.
The righteous recognize an assigned right within their wealth, beginning a direct ethical reversal of the hoarder whom the Fire calls in 70:18.
This verse identifies the claimants to that assigned wealth as the petitioner and the deprived, supplying the needy recipients that complete 70:24’s reversal of withholding.
God “anchors” the mountains, expressing with a different verb the same fixing-to-earth action that underlies the section’s stake dictionary sense.
Choking food and painful punishment follow the shackles and blaze of 73:12; this ayah contributes further distinct forms to the mixed punitive inventory evoked by the section’s whip.
The criminals bound in fetters in 14:49 wear garments of pitch while fire covers their faces; this verse supplies the bodily punishment into which the preceding restraint delivers them.
Whenever the punished try to leave the anguish described in 22:19-21 they are returned and told to taste burning punishment; the verse contributes inescapability to the pour-and-mace scene.
The visiting angels state that they were sent to release stones of clay upon the transgressors, another specific formulation of punishment arriving as many objects from above.
The birds pelt the army with stones of baked clay, staging a collective punitive shower from overhead without using the rain verb.
The hearers are warned that God may send a stone-bearing storm upon them, a close repeated formulation of punishment descending with a storm’s volume.
The people of Shuʿayb are seized by “the punishment of the day of shadow,” locating عذاب in an overhead covering and calling it the punishment of a tremendous day.
The rejecters challenge God to rain stones from the sky or bring painful punishment, explicitly placing a punitive stone-rain and عذاب as parallel demanded outcomes.
Saqar is described as scorching the skin, another precise instance of punishment working upon the bodily surface through which the section explains the whip.
The Fire calls the person who amassed and withheld wealth; this verse supplies the hoarding offense behind the skin-stripping blaze described in 70:15-16.
Jacob requires his sons to give a binding pledge from God before entrusting Benjamin to them, using the و ث ق root for a moral surety meant to secure a person’s return.
The eldest brother recalls the binding pledge their father took from them in 12:66, repeating the root’s nonmaterial sense when that pledged security has failed.
Pharaoh threatens to make Moses one of the imprisoned if he takes another god, an indirect but concrete exercise of the confinement power that the section locates in the stake-holder.
For one unable to complete the preceding stages of expiation, feeding sixty needy people is required; this ayah supplies feeding as the companion restorative act to the release in 58:3.
When Pharaoh’s people provoke divine anger, God exacts retribution and drowns them all, turning the earthly punisher into the object of decisive divine force.
God takes retribution from Pharaoh’s people and drowns them for denying the signs, another explicit formulation of the tyrant’s final reversal.

The blaze is described with الشَّوَى, commonly understood as stripping skin or bodily extremities; on that reading it supplies the bodily surface affected by the punishment, while the term’s exact anatomical range makes the link uncertain.
